steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the analysis section of an encyclopedia article on application permissions: how the permission-based access control model works, its weaknesses, the main criticisms from researchers, and tools that try to improve privacy or transparency.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- The permission-based access control model
- All-or-nothing grants and lack of transparency
- Criticism by researchers
- Data spoofing and transparency tools

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Model
  - assigns access privileges for data objects to applications
  - derivative of discretionary access control
  - granted in context of specific user on specific device; often permanent, few automatic restrictions
- All-or-nothing / transparency
  - sometimes all-or-nothing: grant all requested permissions or barred from the app
  - unclear when each permission is used by a program
  - same transparency problem for accessing the protected data
  - user can revoke, but app can blackmail: refuse to operate, crash, or ask again
- Criticism by researchers
  - intransparency of personal data extraction and surveillance; false sense of security
  - end-user fatigue micro-managing permissions -> fatalistic acceptance of surveillance and intransparency
  - massive data extraction and surveillance after permissions granted, often users unaware
- Tools
  - XPrivacy, Mockdroid spoof data as privacy measure
  - other transparency methods: longitudinal behavioural profiling; multiple-source privacy analysis of app data access

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The permission-based access control model gives applications access privileges for certain data objects. It is derived from the discretionary access control model. Access permissions are usually granted in the context of a specific user on a specific device. Permissions are often granted permanently and there are few automatic restrictions on them.

In some cases permissions use an 'all-or-nothing' approach, where a user is expected to grant all of the requested permissions to be able to access the application, or else the user is completely blocked from using that application. There is still a lack of transparency about exactly when each permission is used by a program or application. The same lack of transparency also applies to accessing the data that is protected by the permission access-control mechanism. Even if the user is able to revoke a permission, the app can blackmail the user by refusing to work, for example by just crashing or by asking the user to grant the permission again to access the application.

- Criticism by researchers
  - intransparency of personal data extraction and surveillance; false sense of security
  - end-user fatigue micro-managing permissions -> fatalistic acceptance of surveillance and intransparency
  - massive data extraction and surveillance after permissions granted, often users unaware
- Tools
  - XPrivacy, Mockdroid spoof data as privacy measure
  - other transparency methods: longitudinal behavioural profiling; multiple-source privacy analysis of app data access

steps.name: rough_draft
draft_citation_needed
steps.text:
The permission-based access control model gives applications access privileges for certain data objects. It is derived from the discretionary access control model. Access permissions are usually granted in the context of a specific user on a specific device. Permissions are often granted permanently and there are few automatic restrictions on them.

In some cases permissions use an 'all-or-nothing' approach, where a user is expected to grant all of the requested permissions to be able to access the application, or else the user is completely blocked from using that application. There is still a lack of transparency about exactly when each permission is used by a program or application. The same lack of transparency also applies to accessing the data that is protected by the permission access-control mechanism. Even if the user is able to revoke a permission, the app can blackmail the user by refusing to work, for example by just crashing or by asking the user to grant the permission again to access the application.

Researchers have criticized the permission mechanism a lot, for several reasons, including;

Intransparency of how personal data is extracted and of surveillance, which includes creating a false sense of security;[citation needed]

End-user fatigue from micro-managing access permissions, which leads to users fatalistically accepting surveillance and intransparency;[citation needed]

Massive data extraction and personal surveillance that happens once the permissions are granted (often by users who do not know that surveillance is happening behind the scenes).[citation needed]

Some apps, like XPrivacy and Mockdroid[citation needed], spoof data as a privacy measure. Other transparency methods include longitudinal behavioural profiling and multiple-source privacy analysis of how apps access data.[citation needed]

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The permission-based access control model assigns access privileges for certain data objects to applications. It is a derivative of the discretionary access control model. Access permissions are usually granted in the context of a specific user on a specific device, and are often granted permanently with few automatic restrictions.

In some cases, permissions are implemented with an 'all-or-nothing' approach: a user is expected either to grant all the requested permissions in order to access the application, or else is completely barred from accessing that application. There is still a lack of transparency about exactly when each permission is used by a given program or application. The same lack-of-transparency concern also applies to accessing the data protected by the permission access-control mechanism. Even if a user can revoke a permission, the app can blackmail the user by refusing to operate, for example by simply crashing or by asking the user to grant the permission again in order to access the application.

The permission mechanism has been widely criticized by researchers for several reasons, including;

Intransparency of personal data extraction and surveillance, including the creation of a false sense of security;[1,2]

End-user fatigue from micro-managing access permissions, leading to a fatalistic acceptance of surveillance and intransparency;[3]

Massive data extraction and personal surveillance carried out once the permissions have been granted (often by users who are unaware that surveillance is taking place behind the scenes).[4,5]

Some apps, such as XPrivacy and Mockdroid[6], spoof data as a privacy measure. Further transparency methods include longitudinal behavioural profiling and multiple-source privacy analysis of app data access.[7,8]
